title: Extreme outbreaks in non-Markovian epidemics on complex networks
abstract: Extreme epidemic risk is controlled by the right tail of the outbreak-size distribution, but this distribution is generally unknown for non-Markovian spreading on networks. Here we determine this distribution by mapping non-Markovian SIR dynamics to an effective Markovian description. We show that arbitrary infection and recovery time statistics can be incorporated through a single edge transmissibility, yielding an effective Markovian process that reproduces the full outbreak-size statistics. For weakly heterogeneous networks, the reduction yields a universal well-mixed semiclassical theory governed by the bond-percolation reproductive number. Outbreak statistics across diverse waiting-time distributions and topologies collapse onto one predictive curve. For highly heterogeneous and empirical networks, the corresponding effective Markovian dynamics on the network captures the complete distribution. Our results provide a direct route from measured waiting-time distributions to quantitative predictions of network-level extreme-outbreak risk.
summary: This work develops a theoretical framework to predict extreme epidemic risk by modeling non-Markovian spreading on complex networks. The core innovation is mapping the system's complex waiting-time statistics onto an equivalent, simpler Markovian process. This allows for quantitative prediction of outbreak size distributions even when infection and recovery times are not exponentially distributed.
main_problem: The primary goal is determining the full outbreak-size distribution, especially its right tail, for non-Markovian epidemic spreading on complex networks.
main_result: The authors show that mapping non-Markovian SIR dynamics to an effective Markovian description allows for quantitative prediction of extreme outbreak risk across diverse network topologies and waiting-time distributions.
method: They map the non-Markovian process to an effective Markovian one using a single edge transmissibility, employing WKB semiclassical theory for large deviations in weakly heterogeneous networks.
model_or_system: The model is based on SIR epidemic dynamics ($S+I+R=N$) generalized from standard Markovian assumptions to include arbitrary waiting-time distributions (e.g., Gamma) for infection and recovery periods on complex networks.
key_observables: Outbreak-size distribution $P(x^*_r)$, mean outbreak fraction ($x^*_r$), conditional standard deviation ($\sigma^*_r$), and the effective per-edge transmissibility ($T$).
important_parameters: Infection/recovery shape parameters ($\alpha_{inf}, \alpha_{rec}$), network heterogeneity quantified by $\sigma_k/ ar{k}$, and the basic reproduction number $R_0$.
main_assumptions: The theory relies on mapping non-Markovian dynamics to an effective Markovian process; universality holds best for weakly heterogeneous networks, where WKB approximations are applicable.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the dependence of transmissibility ($T$) and deterministic outbreak fractions on shape parameters ($\alpha$), demonstrating universal collapse for weak heterogeneity, while supplementary figures compare results across different network types (ER, Gamma, Hamsterster) showing deviations due to degree correlations.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the mapping from non-Markovian to effective Markovian dynamics. It then analyzes outbreak statistics using WKB theory for weakly heterogeneous cases, before extending the framework to highly correlated networks using bond percolation concepts.
why_interesting: While focused on epidemiology, the mathematical techniques—mapping complex stochastic processes (non-Markovian) onto simpler, analytically tractable forms (effective Markovian)—are directly applicable to analyzing open quantum systems or non-equilibrium dynamics in many-body physics.
